procedural_history.originating_court: Unknown (likely a trial court in Andhra Pradesh, based on the High Court's jurisdiction)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 8, 1966, of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 636 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Andhra Pradesh High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 636 of 1963. The final order of the High Court on appeal followed the opinion expressed by Basi Reddy, J. The High Court convicted the appellants on certain charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court granted a temporary restraining order preventing the respondents from opening sluices or cutting breaches to a tank bund. The case before the Supreme Court is Criminal Appeal No. 75 of 1967.

decision.conviction_status: The order of acquittal on other charges is upheld.
decision.sentence_status: The sentences of imprisonment passed on accused 10 are to run concurrently.
directions: I would direct all the sentences of imprisonment passed on accused 10 to run concurrently.
I would uphold the order of acquittal on other charges.

issue.issue_text: The plea of alibi raised by the accused.

facts: Accused No. 10 raised a plea of alibi.
He claimed that on the day of the incident, he was in Sivapuram, Kadapa district, having gone there weeks before.
He stated that he only surrendered to the Magistrate's court after hearing he was named as an accused in the case.
application: The trial court considered the accused's plea of alibi and did not accept it.
The High Court also reviewed and rejected the alibi plea.
The Supreme Court examined the conclusions of both the trial court and the High Court regarding the alibi.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no cogent ground to disagree with the lower courts' conclusion and therefore also rejected the accused's plea of alibi.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court has a duty to consider the right of private defence when there is evidence showing it, even if the plea is not raised by the accused.

facts: Accused no. 10 did not raise the plea of self-defence during his trial.
Instead, accused no. 10 pleaded alibi as his defence.
However, there was evidence and other material on the record which suggested that the circumstances might have justified his actions as an exercise of the right of private defence.
law: The court stated that the technical rules of civil pleadings, such as estoppel, are inappropriate in criminal cases concerning the right of private defence.
The law of private defence is meant to be administered in a practical way with reasonable liberality to fulfill its underlying object, which is preventive, not retributive.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that a court is not prevented from giving an accused the benefit of the right of private defence simply because the accused raised a different plea (like alibi).

The court has a duty to properly appraise all the evidence on record. If this evidence proves that the accused acted in the exercise of the right of private defence, the court would be unjustified in ignoring that evidence and convicting the accused.
The High Court's approach of dismissing the right of private defence because it was not pleaded was deemed erroneous.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a court has a duty to consider the right of private defence if there is evidence on the record to support it, even if the accused has not formally raised that plea and has instead set up a different defence, such as an alibi.

arguments.issue_text: The plea of alibi raised by the accused.
appellant_arguments: The tenth accused put forth a plea of alibi, claiming he was not at the scene of the crime.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution's case was that the tenth accused was present and participated in the incident, thereby refuting the alibi.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court has a duty to consider the right of private defence when there is evidence showing it, even if the plea is not raised by the accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that based on the prosecution's own evidence, they must be held to have acted in the exercise of the right of private defence.

They contended that the prosecution party were the aggressors who came to remove a bund by force and inflicted grievous injuries on several accused persons, justifying their actions to avert further harm.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution argued that their party went to the scene unarmed with the intention of peacefully persuading the accused, and only retaliated after being attacked.
The prosecution's case was that it was proven by overwhelming evidence, which would negate the plea of private defence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The fact that an accused person pleads alibi does not preclude the Court from giving them the benefit of the right of private defence, if the evidence on record concludes that the circumstances gave them the right to act in self-defence.
obiter: The right of private defence of person and property is recognised in all free, civilised, democratic societies within certain reasonable limits.

The analogy of estoppel or of the technical rules of civil pleadings is inappropriate in such cases, and courts are expected to administer the law of private defence in a practical way with reasonable liberality to effectuate its underlying object, which is preventive and not retributive.

Citizens, as a general rule, are neither expected to run away for safety when faced with grave and imminent danger to their person or property as a result of unlawful aggression, nor are they expected, by use of force, to right the wrongs done to them.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court is not precluded from giving an accused the benefit of the right of private defence, even if the accused did not raise that plea and instead pleaded alibi. If, upon a proper appraisal of the evidence and other material on record, the court concludes that the circumstances gave the accused the right to act in self-defence, it would be unjustified in ignoring that evidence and convicting the accused merely because a different defence was formally set up.
legal_tests_applied: When there is evidence proving that a person accused of killing or injuring another acted in the exercise of the right of private defence, the Court is not justified in ignoring that evidence and convicting the accused merely because the latter has set up a defence of alibi and set forth a plea different from the right of private defence.
why_appellant_lost: The plea of alibi raised by the tenth accused was not accepted as the basis for the final decision; the court instead evaluated the evidence on the assumption that he was present and acted in self-defence.
why_respondent_won: The court has a duty to consider the right of private defence if the evidence supports it, even if the accused raises a different plea like alibi, because the technical rules of civil pleadings are inappropriate in criminal cases.

The evidence was sufficient to give rise to a reasonable apprehension in the mind of accused no. 10 that the victims of the assault would have been killed had he not exercised the right of private defence.

The persons against whom the gun was used were the real aggressors, from whom accused no. 10 apprehended grave danger to the lives of the other accused persons and ultimately to himself, thus justifying the use of the gun.
policy_considerations: The analogy of estoppel or of the technical rules of civil pleadings is, in cases like the present, inappropriate.
Courts are expected to administer the law of private defence in a practical way with reasonable liberality so as to effectuate its underlying object.
The essential basic character of the right of private defence is preventive and not retributive.
